question: A developer created a Lightning web component that uses a lightning-record-edit-form to collect information about Leads. Users complain that they only see one error message at a time about their input when trying to save a Lead record. What is the recommended approach to perform validations on more than one field, and display multiple error messages simultaneously with minimal JavaScript intervention?
optionA: Try/catch/finally block
optionB: External JavaScript library
optionC: Validation rules
optionD: Apex trigger
explanation:
Custom validation rules are what Salesforce recommends, and the lightning-record-edit-form documentation says so in as many words: "We recommend using custom validation rules to verify data input instead of implementing client-side validation errors." A single validation rule's formula can evaluate the data in one or more fields, so the multi-field checking this question asks for is expressed declaratively with no JavaScript at all — and because the rule lives on the object, it protects every entry point into the data, not just this component.
The other options are not validation mechanisms. A try/catch/finally block reacts to an error that has already been thrown. An external JavaScript library is the client-side route the documentation explicitly steers you away from. An Apex trigger calling addError() could enforce the same rules, but it is code where configuration already does the job.
One correction to the question's premise, because it is a common misconception: this form does not display several errors at once. Its documentation states that if a single field has multiple validation errors the form shows only the first error on that field, and that if a submitted form has multiple errors it shows only the first error encountered, revealing the next as each is corrected. The "displays all error messages at once" behaviour described in Validation Rule Considerations applies to the standard page-layout UI, not to lightning-record-edit-form. Validation rules are the right answer here because they are the recommended, declarative, multi-field mechanism — not because they change how many messages the component renders.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/lightning-record-edit-form.html
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.fields_validation_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Answer C stands, and is now cited to the sentence that actually settles it: the lightning-record-edit-form guide recommends custom validation rules over client-side validation errors. The explanation was wrong on mechanism, though — it claimed validation rules "display multiple error messages at once on lightning-record-edit-form", and the component's own documentation says the opposite, that a submitted form with multiple errors shows only the first error encountered. The "all messages at once" rule in Validation Rule Considerations describes the standard page-layout UI and was misapplied here.

question: Consider the queries below with this information: More than 200,000 Account records, records include soft-deleted records (in Recycle Bin), and two fields marked as External Id: Customer_Number__c and ERP_Key__c. Which two queries are optimized for large data volumes? Choose 2 answers:
optionA: SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Name != NULL
optionB: SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Name != '' AND Customer_Number__c = 'ValueA'
optionC: SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Id IN :aListVariable
optionD: SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Name != '' AND IsDeleted = false
explanation:
B and C are the optimized queries. Customer_Number__c is marked as an External ID, and Salesforce creates an index on any External ID field, so an equality filter on it is selective. C filters on Id, the primary key, which is always indexed; binding a bounded list of Ids keeps the filter selective. A is not selective: Name != NULL matches essentially every row, so the optimizer falls back to a full table scan. D is not selective either. Name != '' matches nearly every record, and IsDeleted = false adds nothing the optimizer can use, because a SOQL query already excludes soft-deleted rows unless you add ALL ROWS. Selectivity comes from filtering on an indexed field with a narrow result set, not from restating a default.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm

corrected.note: Key B,C is right, but the explanation argued for B and D — it defended an option the key does not name. The LDV Indexes page settles it: External IDs cause an index to be created on that field, and the record Id is the primary key index.

question: Requirements: 1) For mobile devices, information should display in three rows. 2) For desktops and tablets, information should display in a single row. Which option has the correct component code to meet the requirements for desktops and tablets?
optionA: Set size='12' medium-device-size='4'
optionB: Set size='12' medium-device-size='6' large-device-size='4'
optionC: Set size='12' large-device-size='4'
optionD: Set size='12' medium-device-size='6'
explanation:
lightning-layout is a mobile-first 12-column grid. size sets the width at the smallest breakpoint and applies upward until a device-specific attribute overrides it, and the device attributes are additive: small-device-size means a phone, medium-device-size a tablet, large-device-size a desktop, and each applies to the size named and everything larger.
Three items at size='12' each take the full width, so on a phone they stack into three rows — the first requirement. To place all three on a single row from tablet upward, each has to occupy a third of the grid at the medium breakpoint, which is medium-device-size='4'.
The distractors each break one half of the requirement. medium-device-size='6' gives half width, so a tablet shows two items on the first row and the third below it — two rows, not one — and that stays true on desktop because the medium setting carries upward. Adding large-device-size='4' on top of medium-device-size='6' repairs the desktop but leaves the tablet at two per row, and the requirement names tablets explicitly. large-device-size='4' on its own leaves tablets inheriting size='12', so they keep the three-row phone layout.
One thing worth fixing in your mental model: size='12' never produces a single row on any device. Full width means one item per row everywhere, including desktop.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/lightning-layout-item.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/lightning-layout.html

question: A Salesforce org has more than 50,000 contacts. A new business process requires a calculation that aggregates data from all contact records. This calculation needs to run once a day after business hours. Which two steps should a developer take? Choose 2 answers:
optionA: Implement Queueable interface
optionB: Implement Database.Batchable interface
optionC: Implement Schedulable interface
optionD: Use the @future annotation
explanation:
Two requirements, two interfaces, and they are doing different jobs. Database.Batchable carries the volume; Schedulable supplies the recurrence. The Schedulable class's execute() calls Database.executeBatch() on the Batchable class, and System.schedule() sets it to run after hours.
Queueable loses the volume slot on the query. A queueable job is a single transaction with a single set of governor limits, and the limit on total records retrieved by SOQL queries is 50,000 in asynchronous Apex exactly as it is in synchronous Apex — so being async buys nothing, and selecting every Contact in an org of more than 50,000 fails outright. Heap tells the same story: 12 MB in async, which 50,000 Contact records will not fit inside. Batch Apex escapes this by a documented mechanism rather than by being bigger: if start() returns a Database.QueryLocator, the governor limit for the total number of records retrieved by SOQL queries is bypassed, and a QueryLocator can cover up to 50 million records. Separately, each execute() chunk is a discrete transaction whose governor limits are reset, which is what gives the processing room. Those are two different guarantees, and only Batch Apex offers either.
Queueable can't take the other slot either, which is the likelier place to go wrong on a choose-two. The requirement is a recurring time of day — once a day, after business hours — and a queueable has no vocabulary for that. Its only timing control is System.enqueueJob(queueable, delay), where the delay is a minimum of 0 to 10 minutes and is ignored entirely during Apex testing. There is no recurrence and no time of day in it. Schedulable is the interface that takes a cron expression, through System.schedule() or the Schedule Apex page, and the Apex Scheduler documentation names this pairing directly: it is "ideal for daily or weekly maintenance tasks using Batch Apex".
The @future annotation is the weakest option: it can't be scheduled, returns no job id, can't be chained, and accepts only primitives and collections of primitives as arguments. The 50 usually quoted alongside @future is the maximum number of future methods allowed per Apex invocation — a cap on how many future calls one transaction can make, not a cap on records per call.
One detail that catches people out: scheduled Apex is asynchronous, but synchronous governor limits apply to a scheduled job. Schedulable on its own therefore buys no headroom, which is exactly why the Batchable half of this answer is required and not merely tidier.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_batch_interface.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_scheduler.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_queueing_jobs.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_gov_limits.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_annotation_future.htm

question: Universal Containers wants to notify an external system when an unhandled exception occurs in their nightly Apex batch job. What is the appropriate publish/subscribe logic?
optionA: Have the external system subscribe to a custom Platform Event that gets fired with addError()
optionB: Have the external system subscribe to a custom Platform Event that gets fired with EventBus.publish()
optionC: Have the external system subscribe to a standard Platform Event that gets fired with EventBus.publish()
optionD: Have the external system subscribe to a standard Platform Event that gets fired
explanation:
BatchApexErrorEvent is a standard platform event that the platform publishes on your behalf. The Apex Developer Guide states that if the start, execute, or finish method of a batch Apex job encounters an unhandled exception, a BatchApexErrorEvent is fired, and that to get this behaviour the batch class declaration must implement the Database.RaisesPlatformEvents marker interface. The event's own reference page then settles the rest of the option set in a single line: "Only the Salesforce Platform can fire this event; Apex code and the API can't." That rules out every option built on publishing the event yourself, whether the option calls the event custom or standard.
The same page lists the supported subscribers as Apex triggers, flows, processes, the Pub/Sub API, and the Streaming API (CometD), so an external system genuinely can listen on the /event/BatchApexErrorEvent channel. It receives the AsyncApexJob id, the exception type and message, the stack trace, and the record ids that were in scope at the time of failure.
There is also a reason no custom-event design could have worked here. An unhandled exception is by definition not caught, so there is no point in your own code at which to publish, and an event published with the default publish-after-commit behaviour is discarded when the transaction rolls back. addError() adds a record-level error inside a trigger and publishes nothing at all.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_batch_platformevents.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/sforce_api_objects_batchapexerrorevent.htm

corrected.note: The Apex Developer Guide documents BatchApexErrorEvent as a standard platform event fired automatically by the platform for unhandled batch exceptions, gated only on implementing Database.RaisesPlatformEvents. No custom event and no EventBus.publish() call is involved, which is what the old key B asserted.

question: A developer has three savepoints SP1, SP2, SP3 (created in order). During execution, code rolls back to SP1, fixes a condition, then tries to roll back to SP3, causing a runtime error. Why?
optionA: SP3 became invalid when SP1 was rolled back
optionB: The developer has too many DML statements between savepoints
optionC: The developer used too many savepoints in one trigger session
optionD: The developer should have called SP2 before calling SP3
explanation:
When you rollback to an earlier savepoint (SP1), it invalidates all savepoints created after it. So rolling back to SP1 automatically invalidates both SP2 and SP3. Trying to rollback to SP3 after this results in a runtime error because SP3 no longer exists.

question: Assuming the CreateOneAccount class implements the Queueable interface, which syntax properly tests the Apex code?
explanation:
A queueable job is asynchronous, so nothing it does is visible to the test until the platform is told to drain the queue. Enclosing System.enqueueJob() in Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest() is what forces that: every asynchronous process started inside the block runs synchronously when Test.stopTest() is reached, so an assertion placed after it sees the job's results.
Each of the other three fails for its own reason. Enqueuing with no start/stop block at all leaves the job sitting in the queue when the query runs, so the assertion tests the state of the org before the job ever executed. Putting the assertion inside the block, before Test.stopTest(), has exactly the same effect — it is the stopTest() call that drains the queue, not startTest(), so an assertion above it is still running too early. And Database.executeBatch() is the entry point for a class implementing Database.Batchable; handing it a Queueable does not compile, because the two interfaces are unrelated.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_queueing_jobs.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_tools_start_stop_test.htm

question:
A developer created a Lightning web component that uses a Lightning_record_edit_fom to collect Information about Leads. Users complain that they only see one error message at a time about their input when trying to save a Lead record.
Which best practice should the developer use to perform the validations on more than one held, thus allowing more than one error message to be displayed simultaneously?
optionA: Apex REST
optionB: Client_side validation
optionC: Custom validation rules
optionD: Next Best Action
explanation:
Custom validation rules are the documented recommendation, and the lightning-record-edit-form guide states the comparison this question is built on directly: "We recommend using custom validation rules to verify data input instead of implementing client-side validation errors." A validation rule's formula can evaluate the data in one or more fields, which is the multi-field validation the question asks for, and it is enforced on the object — so it holds for the API, Data Loader, flows and every other UI, not only for this component. Client-side validation reimplements business rules in JavaScript, protects one entry point, and is what the guide tells you not to do.
Apex REST is an inbound integration mechanism and Next Best Action serves recommendations; neither validates form input.
Be careful with the premise, though. Reaching for validation rules will not, on its own, produce several error messages side by side. The component's documentation states that if a single field has multiple validation errors the form shows only the first error on that field, and that if a submitted form has multiple errors it shows only the first error encountered, showing the next one as each is corrected. The "displays all error messages at once" statement in Validation Rule Considerations describes the standard page-layout UI. If the requirement is genuinely to surface several problems in one pass, the honest answer is to write one rule whose formula covers the related fields and whose message names them together.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/lightning-record-edit-form.html
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.fields_validation_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question:
Universal Containers uses a custom Lightning page to provide a mechanism to perform a step-by-step wizard search for Accounts. One of the steps in the wizard is to allow the user to input text into a text field, ERF Number_c, that is then used in a query to find matching Accounts. 
erpNumber = + '%';
List<Account> accounts = [SELECT Id,Name FROM Account WHERE ERP_Number__c LIKE :erpNumber]
The query needs to be optimized, Which option whould be best?
optionA: Perform the SOQL query as part of a for loop.
optionB: Mark the ERP_Numker = field as an external Id
optionC: Mark the ERP_Number__ c field as required.
optionD: Move the SO0L query to within an asynchronous process.
explanation:
Answer: B (Mark the ERP_Number__c field as an External ID)
Why B is correct: External ID automatically creates a database index, which dramatically speeds up the LIKE query by allowing the database to quickly find matching records instead of scanning all Account records.
Why others are wrong:

question:
A company processes Orders within their Salesforce instance. When an Order's status changes to 'Paid' it must notify the company's order management system
(OMS). The OMS exposes SOAP web service endpoints to listen for when to retrieve the data from Salesforce.
What is the optimal method to implement this?
optionA: Generate the Enterprise WSDL and use it to make a callout to the OMS.
optionB: Generate the Partner WSDL and use it to make a callout to the OMS.
optionC: Create an Outbound Message that contains the session ID and send it to the OMS.
optionD: Create an Apex trigger and make a callout to the OMS from the trigger.
explanation:
Outbound messaging is the right mechanism here. It is declarative, it fires from a workflow rule, flow, or approval process when the Order's status changes to Paid, it delivers a SOAP message to an endpoint of the kind the OMS already exposes, and it retries on its own: messages queue until they are delivered or until they are 24 hours old, with a 60-second timeout per attempt. Generating the Enterprise or Partner WSDL is backwards, because those WSDLs describe Salesforce's own API for clients calling in, not the OMS's endpoint. A callout from an Apex trigger works but has to be made asynchronously, consumes the transaction's callout budget, and makes you hand-build the retry behaviour outbound messaging already provides.
One detail in this item is now out of date. Outbound messages no longer carry a session id. Effective the week of 23 February 2026, Salesforce removed the Send Session ID option, forced IncludeSessionId to false, and stopped including the sessionID element in the payload; a system that calls back into Salesforce after receiving the notification must authenticate with OAuth 2.0. Choose the outbound message for the declarative, retrying SOAP delivery, not for a session id it no longer sends.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.workflow_om_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.workflow_managing_outbound_messages.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=005232763&language=en_US&type=1

question:
A developer is asked to update data in an org based on new business rules. The new rules state that Accounts with the type set to 'Customer' should have a status of 'Active', and Accounts with the type set to 'Prospect' should have a status of 'Pending'. No other changes to data should be made.
Which code block will accurately meet the business requirements?
explanation:
Both A and B write the correct Status values, so the field values are not what separates them — read the placement of accountUpdates.add(a) instead.
In B the query itself is scoped: WHERE Type IN :statusMap.keySet() retrieves only Customers and Prospects, every record retrieved is one the rules apply to, and the new value comes straight out of the map with statusMap.get(a.Type), so the mapping is stated once.
In A the add() sits outside the containsKey guard, so every Account in the org lands in accountUpdates and the DML writes to all of them. The guard protects the field values but not the update. That matters in three concrete ways. Every one of those unrelated Accounts runs its update triggers, flows, and validation rules, so a single validation rule failing on a record that has nothing to do with this change fails the entire DML and nothing is updated at all. Their audit fields move even though no business field did. And the code does not survive volume: the unfiltered query is capped at 50,000 rows and the update at 10,000 records per transaction, so in an org large enough to care about this task, A throws before it finishes while B stays bounded by the number of Customers and Prospects.
C has the same defect as A in a more verbose form. D is the one that is wrong on values as well: it sets every Account whose Type is not 'Customer' — including Accounts with no Type at all — to 'Pending'.
The habit being tested is to scope the query to the records the requirement names, rather than querying everything and sorting it out in Apex.

https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_gov_limits.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_bulk.htm

Both blocks assign the correct statuses, but in A the accountUpdates.add(a) call sits outside the containsKey guard, so the DML touches every Account in the org — which the stem's 'no other changes to data should be made' forbids, and which hits the 10,000-row DML and 50,000-row SOQL governor limits at scale. <!-- Lightning Web Component HTML file -->

<template>
    <lightning-button label="Call server" onclick={handleClick}></lightning-button>

export default class HelloWorld extends LightningElement {
    firstName = 'World';
    
    handleClick() {
        serverEcho({ firstName: this.firstName })
            .then((result) => {
                alert('From Server: ' + result);
            })
            .catch((error) => {
                console.error(error);
            });
    }
}

// Apex Controller for Lightning Component

public with sharing class SimpleServerSideController {
    @AuraEnabled
    public static String serverEcho(Object firstName) {
        String firstNameStr = (String)firstName.get('firstName');
        return ('Hello from the server, ' + firstNameStr);
    }
}
Given the code above, which two changes need to be made in the Apex Controller for the code to work?
optionA: Annotate the entire class as @AuraEnabled instead of just the single method.
optionB: Change the argument in the Apex Controller line 05 from subject to string.
optionC: Change the method signature to be global static, not public to String.
optionD: Remove line 06 from the Apex Controller and instead use firstName in the return on line 07.
explanation:
The component calls serverEcho({ firstName: this.firstName }), and an imperative Apex call passes an object whose property names match the Apex method's parameter names. So the Apex parameter has to be named firstName and typed to what the component actually sends — a String. Declaring it as Object is what breaks the call.
Once the parameter is a String, line 06 has nothing left to do: firstName already holds the value, and .get('firstName') is a Map operation that a String does not have. Remove that line and return firstName directly.
The other two options are wrong on their own terms. @AuraEnabled goes on the method, not on the class — annotating the class does not expose anything. And an @AuraEnabled method already has to be static and public or global, so switching it to global changes nothing about the argument that is actually failing.

optionA: SELECT Account__c, Program__c, Transaction_Date__c FROM Customer_Transaction__b WHERE Account__c = '001R000000302D3' AND Program__c ='Shoppers' AND Transaction_Date__c=2019-05-31T00:00Z

optionC: SELECT Account__c, Program__c, Transaction_Date__c FROM Customer_Transaction__b WHERE Account__c = '001R000000302D3' AND Program__c INCLUDES ('Shoppers', 'Womens') AND Transaction_Date__c=2019-05-31T00:00Z

question: which use case can only be performed by using asynchronous apex

optionB: Processing high volumes of records
optionC: Updating a record after the completion of an insert
optionD: Calling a web service from an Apex trigger
explanation:
A trigger runs synchronously, and Salesforce does not permit a synchronous callout from trigger context — attempting one raises "Callout from triggers are currently not supported". The only way to call a web service from a trigger is to hand the work to asynchronous Apex: an @future(callout=true) method or a Queueable. That makes this a use case where synchronous Apex is not merely slower but forbidden.
Processing high volumes and updating a record after an insert are both done synchronously every day; volume pushes you toward Batch Apex for governor headroom, not because a synchronous approach is impossible.
Option A is the weak distractor here and worth naming: scheduling a batch to run later does require the Schedulable interface, which is itself asynchronous Apex, so read literally it is also something "only performed by asynchronous Apex". The discriminator the item is reaching for is the callout, where a synchronous attempt is actively rejected by the platform rather than merely unavailable.

question:
A developer has a test class that creates test data before making a mock callout but now receives a 'You have uncommitted work pending. Please commit or rollback before calling out' error.
Which step should be taken to resolve the error?
optionA: Ensure both the Insertion and mock callout occur after the I==L. stoptest_().
optionB: Ensure the records are Inserted before the Tezt.startTest() statement and the mock callout occurs within a method annotated with @testSetup.
optionC: Ensure both the insertion and mock callout occur after the Test.startTest().
optionD: Ensure the records are inserted before the Test.startTess() statement and the mock callout occurs after the Test. Startest().
explanation:
The Apex Developer Guide states the rule and its workaround in one place: callouts aren't allowed after DML operations in the same transaction, because the DML leaves pending uncommitted work. To insert test data and still make a mock callout, enclose the callout in Test.startTest and Test.stopTest and keep the DML outside that block — so the inserts run before Test.startTest and the callout runs after it. The same page adds that Test.startTest must appear before Test.setMock.
Two things are worth stating precisely. Test.startTest does not commit the inserted records; nothing in a test is ever committed. It opens a fresh context with its own set of governor limits, and it is that boundary the callout restriction is evaluated against. And the rule is not that every callout must precede every DML statement — DML that happens after a mock callout is explicitly allowed and needs no special handling.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_restful_http_testing_dml.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm

The guide's rule is that the callout goes inside Test.startTest/Test.stopTest while the DML stays outside it.

explanation:
Breaking the query in two is the documented remedy. The Large Data Volumes best-practices guide names this exact case: if you use two indexed fields joined by an OR in the WHERE clause, the result set can exceed the index selectivity threshold, so decompose the query — run it as two queries and join the results. Each half then filters on a single indexed field and can use that index, and the union of the two result sets is the same set of Accounts the OR would have returned, which is what 'preserving the entire result set' requires.
A formula field does not help: a formula combining CreatedDate and RecordTypeId is evaluated at query time, and a non-deterministic formula field can't be indexed at all. @Future moves the same slow query into another transaction without making it any faster. Database.getQueryLocator is how Batch Apex streams a large result set, but it does not change the query's selectivity — the same non-selective OR is still evaluated, so it addresses row limits rather than the performance problem described here.

optionA: Annotate the Apex method with @AuraEnabled.
optionB: . Implement the with sharing keyword in the class declaration.
optionC: . Implement the with keyword in the class declaration.
optionD: Use the WZ E D clause within the SOQL query.
explanation:
Three changes, each doing a different job. `@AuraEnabled` exposes the method to the component at all (A). `@AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)` is what makes it wire-callable and lets the framework cache the result on the client, which is the "efficiently" half of the requirement (E) — a plain `@AuraEnabled` method can only be called imperatively. And `with sharing` on the class declaration is the security half (B).

Be precise about what `with sharing` actually buys, because it is narrower than it sounds. It enforces the running user's **record-level** access — org-wide defaults, the role hierarchy, sharing rules, manual and Apex shares — so the query stops returning Leads the user has no right to see. It does **not** enforce their object or field permissions: "Enforcing sharing rules by using the with sharing keyword doesn't enforce the user's permissions and field-level security." A user with no read access to AnnualRevenue still gets that field back from a `with sharing` class.

Closing that second gap is a separate change. The modern mechanism is a user-mode query — `WITH USER_MODE` on the SOQL, or `Security.stripInaccessible` on the result — which enforces object permissions and FLS alongside sharing. Option D looks like a scrape-mangled attempt at exactly that clause ("WZ E D" for `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED`, the older form of the same idea); as printed it is unreadable, so treat B as the record-access answer rather than a complete security answer.

Option C names no real keyword — the declaration is `with sharing`, `without sharing`, or `inherited sharing`.

One version note: from API version 67.0 Apex database operations run in user mode by default, and a class containing `@AuraEnabled` methods that declares no sharing keyword already uses an implicit `with sharing`. Declaring the keyword explicitly, as this item asks, is still the right habit because it keeps the class's behaviour stable across API versions.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/apex-wire-method.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_keywords_sharing.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_security_sharing_rules.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_enforce_usermode.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/apex-security.html

corrected.note: Answer stands. The explanation claimed the `with sharing` keyword "ensures that the data access is enforced according to the user's permissions" — the Apex Developer Guide says the opposite, that `with sharing` does not enforce the user's permissions or field-level security. It governs record access only; FLS needs a user-mode query or stripInaccessible. Option D also appears to be a scrape-mangled `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` clause and is unreadable as printed.

question: Part of a custom Lightning Component displays the total number of Opportunities in the org, which is in the millions. The Lightning Component uses an Apex Controller to get the data it needs. What is the optimal way for a developer to get the total number of Opportunities for the Lightning Component?
optionA: Apex Batch job that counts the number of Opportunity records
optionB: SUM() SOQL aggregate query on the Opportunity object
optionC: SOQL for loop that counts the number of Opportunities records
optionD: COUNT() SOQL aggregate query on the Opportunity object
explanation:
COUNT() asks the database for a number rather than for records, and the Apex Developer Guide is precise about what that costs: for COUNT() and COUNT(fieldName), limits are counted as one query row — unless the query carries a GROUP BY, in which case one query row per grouping is consumed. So counting millions of Opportunities spends a single row against the 50,000-row query limit.
The same passage is what really rules out SUM(). Every aggregate function other than COUNT() and COUNT(fieldName) counts each row used by the aggregation as a query row, so SUM() over millions of Opportunities would exceed the 50,000-row limit outright — quite apart from totalling a currency field instead of counting records. A SOQL for loop retrieves the records it iterates, and a batch job is asynchronous and far heavier than one query for a number the component needs in order to render.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.soql_sosl.meta/soql_sosl/sforce_api_calls_soql_select_count.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_SOQL_agg_fns.htm

question: What is the transaction limit for the number of records per DML statement?
explanation:
The number is 10,000, and the precise wording matters: Execution Governors and Limits states it as the total number of records processed as a result of DML statements in a transaction, not an allowance per statement. Ten inserts of 1,000 records each exhaust it exactly as a single insert of 10,000 would, and records touched by cascading automation — triggers, flows, roll-up recalculations — count against the same total. That is why a mass update can fail on this limit even though no individual DML statement comes close to 10,000 rows.
The companion limit is 150 DML statements per transaction. Both are transaction-wide and both are the same in synchronous and asynchronous contexts.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_gov_limits.htm

corrected.note: Answer D (10,000) stands. The explanation described it as a per-statement ceiling — 'in a single DML operation you can process up to 10,000 records at once' — but the governor is the total number of records processed by DML across the whole transaction. The deck's own cascading-trigger question depends on the transaction-wide reading, so the two explanations contradicted each other.

question: A developer created a new trigger that inserts a Task when a new Lead is created. After deploying to production, an outside integration is periodically reporting errors. Which change should the developer make to ensure the integration is not affected with minimal impact to business logic?
optionA: Remove the Apex Class from the Integration User's Profile.
optionB: Use the Database method with allOrNone set to False.
optionC: Use a Try/Catch block after the insert statement.
optionD: Deactivate the Trigger before the Integration runs.
explanation:
Inside the trigger, inserting the Task with a Database method using allOrNone=false (e.g., Database.insert(tasks, false)) lets the Lead — and therefore the integration — still commit even if an individual Task insert fails, instead of throwing an exception that rolls back the whole transaction. Removing the class from the integration user (A) or deactivating the trigger (D) skips the logic entirely, and a try/catch alone (C) still rolls back the DML.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_methods_system_database.htm

question:
An environment has two Apex Triggers: 
an after-update trigger on Account and an after-update trigger on Contact.
The Account after-update trigger fires whenever an Account's address is updated, and it updates every associated Contact with that address. 
The Contact after-update trigger fires on every edit, and it updates every Campaign Member record related to the Contact with the Contact's state. 
Consider the following: A mass update of 200 Account records' addresses, where each Account has 50 Contacts. Each Contact has 1 Campaign Member. This means there are 10,000 Contact records across the Accounts and 10,000 Campaign Member records across the contacts. What will happen when the mass update occurs?
optionA: The mass update will fail, since the two triggers fire in the same context, thus exceeding the number of records processed by DML statements.
optionB: There will be no error, since each trigger fires within its own context and each trigger does not exceed the limit of the number of records processed by DML statements.
optionC: There will be no error, since the limit on the number of records processed by DML statements is 50,000.
optionD: The mass update of Account address will succeed, but the Contact address updates will fail due to exceeding number of records processed by DML statements.
explanation:
All cascading DML runs in a single transaction that shares the limit of 10,000 records processed by DML statements. The update of 200 Accounts cascades to 10,000 Contact updates, which cascade to 10,000 Campaign Member updates — roughly 20,200 records processed by DML in one transaction, exceeding the 10,000 limit. The triggers don't each receive a fresh limit, so the mass update fails.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_gov_limits.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_transaction.htm

optionC: C. <apex:pageMessage severity="info" />
optionD: D. <apex:pageMessages />
explanation:
Messages added with ApexPages.addMessage() are rendered by <apex:pageMessages />, which displays all page-level messages with standard Salesforce styling. <apex:message> (A) shows a single message tied to a specific component, and the other tags don't render controller-added messages.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_compref_pageMessages.htm

question: A developer is writing code that requires making callouts to an external web service. Which scenario necessitates that the callout be made in an @future method?
optionA: The callouts will be made in an Apex Trigger.
optionB: The callouts will be made in an Apex Test class.
optionC: The callout could take longer than 60 seconds to complete.
optionD: Over 10 callouts will be made in a single transaction.
explanation:
Triggers execute synchronously and cannot make synchronous callouts, so a callout invoked from trigger logic must be moved to an asynchronous @future(callout=true) (or Queueable) method. A long-running callout (C) is governed by the timeout limit, a test (B) requires mocking rather than @future, and the 10-callouts-per-transaction limit (D) isn't solved by @future.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_annotation_future.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm

question: Sometimes events on Salesforce need to be handled by an external system due to the scale or type of process being executed. Consider the use case of a user in Salesforce needing to get pricing for an order they are building in Salesforce while on the phone with a customer. The pricing logic already exists in a third-party system. Instead of recreating this logic in Salesforce, it will be leveraged by making a request of the third-party system. The response, in this case the pricing, will be returned and stored back in Salesforce. What is the optimal solution?
optionA: A Visualforce page that can make a real-time Apex callout to display and save the pricing back in Salesforce
optionB: An Apex trigger that upon saving the Order will make a real-time Apex callout, saving the pricing back in Salesforce
optionC: A Process Builder process and Outbound Message to fetch the pricing upon save and store the pricing in Salesforce
optionD: An ETL tool to process batches of newly saved Orders every few minutes to store the pricing back in Salesforce
explanation:
This is the Request and Reply pattern, which the integration patterns guide defines as Salesforce invoking a process on a remote system, waiting for that process to complete, and then tracking state based on the response. Every clause of the requirement matches: the rep is on the phone, the pricing has to come back during that interaction, and the returned price is stored on the record.
A Visualforce page whose controller makes a synchronous Apex callout is how you implement that — the user acts, the controller calls the pricing service, and the response is displayed and saved in the same request.
The alternatives all break the synchronous requirement. A callout from a trigger has to be made asynchronously, so the result cannot come back into the page the user is looking at, and it fires on save rather than while the order is being built. An outbound message is Fire and Forget: Salesforce hands the message off and does not wait for a reply, so nothing comes back to display. An ETL job introduces minutes of delay, which is the opposite of what a live phone call needs.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts.htm

question: A company represents their customers as Accounts that have an External ID field called Customer_Number__c. They have a custom Order (Order__c) object, with a Lookup to Account, to represent Orders that are placed in their external order management system (OMS). When an order is fulfilled in the OMS, a REST call to Salesforce should be made that creates an Order record in Salesforce and relates it to the proper Account. What is the optimal way to implement this?
optionA: Perform a REST GET on the Account and a REST POST to update the Order__c with the Account's record ID.
optionB: Perform a REST PATCH to upsert the Order__c and specify the Account's Customer_Number__c in it.
optionC: Perform a REST POST to update the Order__c and specify the Account's Customer_Number__c in it.
optionD: Perform a REST GET on the Account and a REST PATCH to upsert the Order__c with the Account's record ID.
explanation:
B: Perform a REST PATCH to upsert the Order__c and specify the Account's Customer_Number__c in it.
Here's why:
Key Requirements:

Create a new Order record
Relate it to the correct Account using External ID (Customer_Number__c)
Do this efficiently from external system

Why Option B is Optimal:
✅ Single API call - Most efficient, reduces network overhead
✅ External ID reference - Salesforce allows you to reference a Lookup field using the parent's External ID:
json{
  "Account__r": {
    "Customer_Number__c": "CUST-12345"
  },
  "Order_Amount__c": 1000
}
✅ PATCH with upsert - Though creating new, PATCH is appropriate for upsert operations
✅ No need to query Account first - Salesforce handles the lookup automatically
Why Other Options Are Suboptimal:
Option A (GET + POST):

❌ Two API calls instead of one
❌ Unnecessary complexity

Option C (POST only):

❌ POST typically doesn't support the External ID relationship syntax as cleanly
❌ Less idiomatic for this use case

Option D (GET + PATCH):

❌ Two API calls - inefficient
❌ Requires retrieving Account ID first

Best Practice: Salesforce REST API supports referencing parent records via External ID fields using the __r relationship notation, making Option B the most efficient single-call solution.
Answer: B
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/dome_upsert.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/langCon_apex_dml_nested_object.htm

question: What are three benefits of using static resources in Visualforce and Lightning Components? (Choose three.)
optionA: Static resource files are automatically minified.
optionB: Static resource files can be referenced by using the $Resource global variable instead of hardcoded IDs.
optionC: Static resource files can be packaged into a collection of related files in a zip or jar archive.
optionD: Static resource files do not count against an organization's quota of data storage.
optionE: Relative paths can be used in files in static resource archives to refer to other content within the archive.
explanation:
The Visualforce guide names three reasons to prefer a static resource over uploading a file to the Documents tab, and they are the three to select: you can reference the resource by name with the $Resource global variable instead of hard-coding a document id, you can package a directory hierarchy of related files and upload it as a single .zip or .jar archive, and files inside an archive can refer to one another by relative path.
Automatic minification is not one of them — a static resource is served as you uploaded it, so minified JavaScript has to be minified before upload.
The storage option is a flaw in the item rather than a distractor, because it is also true. Salesforce's Data and File Storage Allocations page lists what counts toward file storage — attachments, Files home, CRM Content, Chatter files, the Documents tab, the File field on Knowledge articles, and Site.com assets — and then enumerates data storage object by object. Static resources appear in neither list. They carry their own separate allocation instead: 5 MB per resource and 250 MB per org. So four of the five statements here are correct while only three can be chosen; the three above are the ones the documentation frames as reasons to use the feature, which is what the question asks for.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_resources.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/create-resources.html
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.overview_storage.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Answer B,C,E stands as the three benefits the Visualforce guide itself lists, but the item is defective: option D is also true. Data and File Storage Allocations includes static resources in neither the file-storage list nor the data-storage list, and the Visualforce guide gives them a separate 5 MB per-resource / 250 MB per-org allocation, so they genuinely do not count against the data storage quota. This supersedes the earlier note, which had established only that the deck's original claim ("they do count against the org's file storage") was unsupported; the deeper check shows the opposite statement is the documented one.

question:
A company has a custom object, Sales Demo Request, that has a lookup to an Opportunity. It is required that a Sales Demo Request record be created when an

Opportunity's Probability is greater than 50%.

What is the optimal way to automate this?
optionA: Use an Apex Trigger on Opportunity.
optionB: Build a Flow on Opportunity.
optionC: Create a Workflow on Opportunity.
optionD: Build a Process on Opportunity.
explanation:
A record-triggered Flow on Opportunity can evaluate Probability and create the related Sales Demo Request record declaratively — the optimal no-code approach. Workflow rules (C) can't create custom records (only tasks/field updates), Process Builder (D) can but is being retired in favor of Flow, and an Apex trigger (A) is unnecessary code for a simple declarative requirement.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_build_data_update.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=001096524&language=en_US&type=1

question: A company represents their customers as Accounts in Salesforce. All customers have a unique Customer_Number__c that is unique across all of the company's systems. They also have a custom Invoice__c object, with a Lookup to Account, to represent invoices that are sent out from their external system. This company wants to integrate invoice data back into Salesforce so Sales Reps can see when a customer is paying their bills on time. What is the optimal way to implement this?
optionA: Ensure Customer_Number__c is an External ID and that a custom field Invoice_Number__c is an External ID and Upsert invoice data nightly.
optionB: Query the Account Object upon each call to insert invoice data to fetch the Salesforce ID corresponding to the Customer Number on the invoice.
optionC: Create a cross-reference table in the custom invoicing system with the Salesforce Account ID of each Customer and insert invoice data nightly.
optionD: Use Salesforce Connect and external data objects to seamlessly import the invoice data into Salesforce without custom code.
explanation:
Marking Customer_Number__c as an External ID lets the integration relate each Invoice__c to the correct Account by that key, and adding an External ID on Invoice__c lets a nightly upsert insert new invoices and update existing ones idempotently — without first querying Salesforce for record Ids. Querying per call (B) and cross-reference tables (C) add overhead, and Salesforce Connect (D) surfaces external data live rather than importing it.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/dome_upsert.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm

question: In which of the following scenarios would it be acceptable to use programmatic sharing instead of declarative sharing? (Choose three.)
optionA: Every record created by sales users needs to be visible to their respective manager
optionB: Poor performance when using native sharing components
optionC: Team functionality is required on custom objects
optionD: There is an existing, external system of truth for user access assignments which will continue to drive access and be integrated with salesforce
optionE: You need to change record access to read/write for all users utilising a lightning component
explanation:
The governing principle is in Salesforce's platform sharing architecture guidance: Apex managed sharing, also called programmatic sharing, is for building sharing settings in code when a data access requirement can't be met by any other means. Read the options against that test.
Team functionality on custom objects qualifies, because account, opportunity, and case teams exist only on those standard objects — there is no declarative team feature to turn on for a custom object, so the share records have to be created in code.
An external system that owns user access assignments qualifies too. Declarative sharing is driven by ownership, role, and field criteria inside Salesforce; none of those can be driven by an outside system of record, so an integration writing share rows programmatically is the only route.
Performance at scale is the softest of the three, and worth flagging as such: it is a real consideration — large volumes of sharing rules make group membership recalculation expensive — but it is a judgement about scale rather than a capability the declarative model lacks.
The two rejected options fail the test outright. A manager seeing records created by their team is precisely what the role hierarchy does declaratively. Granting read/write to all users is an organization-wide default change, not a sharing design problem, and has nothing to do with the component displaying the records.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/fundamentals/platform-sharing-architecture
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm

question: How long is field history retained?
optionA: 18 Months
optionB: 12 Months
optionC: 24 Months
optionD: 6 Months
explanation:
Standard field history tracking retains data for up to 18 months in the org (visible in the UI) and up to 24 months via the API; the commonly cited answer is 18 months. Longer retention requires the paid Field Audit Trail feature.

https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.tracking_field_history.htm&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.field_audit_trail.htm&type=5

question: Customer billing data must be added and updated into Salesforce from a remote system on weekly basis. Additionally, customer activity information must be extracted from Salesforce and put it into an on-premises data warehouse on a weekly basis. Which approach should be used to import data into Salesforce and export data out of Salesforce, taking into consideration that these imports and exports can interfere with end-user operations during business hours and involve large amounts of data?
optionA: Batch Apex, where Salesforce pushes data to and pulls data from the remote systems
optionB: Replication via third-party ETL to push data into Salesforce and pull data out in batches
optionC: Salesforce Connect to push data to and pull data from the remote systems
optionD: Call-in directly from each remote system to Salesforce APIs to push and pull the data
explanation:
This is Batch Data Synchronization, which the integration patterns guide defines as data in Salesforce being created or refreshed to reflect updates from an external system, and changes from Salesforce being sent to an external system, with updates in either direction done in a batch manner. The requirement is bidirectional and weekly, which is that definition almost word for word.
A third-party ETL tool is the standard implementation: it can be scheduled outside business hours so the load doesn't compete with users, it moves large volumes through the Bulk API, and it handles both directions with one tool.
The alternatives each miss part of it. Batch Apex runs inside Salesforce and can push data out, but nothing about it pulls a weekly extract from a remote billing system on its own. Salesforce Connect is data virtualization — it reads external data live rather than replicating it, so the warehouse still doesn't get its copy. Direct API calls from each remote system can move the data but leave you building and scheduling the orchestration for every system separately, which is what an ETL tool exists to avoid.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm

question: Which scenario requires a developer to use an Apex callout instead of Outbound Messaging?
optionA: The target system uses a REST API.
optionB: The callout needs to be asynchronous.
optionC: The target system uses a SOAP API.
optionD: The callout needs to be invoked from a Workflow Rule.
explanation:
Outbound Messaging only supports SOAP, so when the target system exposes a REST API you must use an Apex HTTP callout. Asynchronous delivery (B) and invocation from a workflow rule (D) are actually strengths of outbound messaging, and a SOAP target (C) is exactly what outbound messaging handles.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.workflow_managing_outbound_messages.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts.htm

question: As part of a new integration, a developer is asked to implement a new custom search functionality that is capable of performing unrestricted queries and can account for all values within a custom picklist field, Typec, on the Opportunity object. The search feature must also account for NULL values. The organization-wide default for the Opportunity object is set to Public Read-Only, and a new custom index has been created for the Typec field. There are more than 5 million Opportunity records within the environment, and a considerable amount of the existing records have NULL values for the picklist. Which technique should the developer implement to maximize performance when querying NULL values?
optionA: Use a SOSL query to return ALL opportunities that have a value of NULL in any field.
optionB: Use the OR operator to combine WHERE clauses to strictly search for each value within the picklist, including Typec = NULL.
optionC: Perform two SOQL queries; one to query Opportunities where Typec != NULL, and another to query where Type__c = NULL, then join the result set using Apex.
optionD: Create a formula field that substitutes NULL values for a string of text, create an index for the formula field, then use the formula within the WHERE clause.
explanation:
The query optimizer can't use a standard index to find NULL values efficiently. Creating a formula field that converts NULLs to a concrete string, indexing that formula field, and filtering on it lets the optimizer use the index and still return the full result set (including former NULLs) selectively against 5M+ records. SOSL (A) doesn't fit, OR-combining every value (B) is non-selective, and splitting into two queries (C) leaves the NULL query non-selective.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_soql_and_sosl.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm

question: As part of a custom interface, a developer team creates various new Lightning web components. Each of the components handles errors using toast messages. When the development is complete, all the components are added to the same Lightning page. During acceptance testing, users complain about the long chain of toast messages that display when errors occur loading the components. Which two techniques should the developer implement to improve the user experience? (Choose two.)
optionA: Use a [template] tag to display in-place error messages
optionB: Use public properties on each component to display the error messages
optionC: Use the window.alert() method to display the error messages.
optionD: Use a Lightning web component to aggregate and display all errors.
explanation:
To avoid a chain of stacked toasts, display errors inline within each component using a conditional <template> block (A), and/or use a single dedicated component to aggregate and present all errors together (D). Public properties (B) don't address the toast spam, and window.alert() (C) produces even more disruptive blocking popups.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/apex-error-handling.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/create-conditional.html

optionA: import getOrders from '@salesforce/apex/OrderController.getAvailableOrders';
optionB: import getOrders from '@salesforce/apex/c.OrderController.getAvailableOrders';
optionC: import { LightningElement, api ) from 'lwc';
optionD: import { LighningElement, wire } from 'lwc';
explanation:
Two issues block deployment: the Apex import must use the full @salesforce/apex/ path — import getOrders from '@salesforce/apex/OrderController.getAvailableOrders'; (A) — and because the code uses the @wire decorator, wire must be imported from lwc: import { LightningElement, wire } from 'lwc'; (D). Option B's path (c.OrderController) is wrong, and option C imports api, which the code doesn't need.

question: A developer has a Debug method within a class, which is invoked hundreds of times.What is the optimal functionality in the Developer Console to count the number of calls made to the method?
optionA: A. The "Execution Log" Panel
optionB: The "Execution Stack" Panel
optionC: The "Executed Units" tab under the Execution Overview
optionD: The "Execution Tree" tab under the Stack Tree Panel
explanation:
In the Developer Console's Execution Overview, the "Executed Units" tab aggregates execution by unit (methods, queries, triggers, etc.) and shows how many times each ran and the time spent — the right place to count how often a method was invoked. The other panels show the raw log, call stack, or tree rather than per-method call counts.

https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.code_dev_console_view_system_log.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: During the order of execution of a Visualforce page GET request, what happens after this step?
optionA: Evaluate constructors and expressions on custom components
optionB: Create view state if <apex: form> exists
optionC: Send the HTML response to the browser
optionD: Evaluate expressions, action attributes, and method calls
explanation:
The documented order for a Visualforce get request is: the constructors on the custom controller or controller extensions run first; then any custom components on the page are created, their controllers' constructors run, and the expressions set on their attributes are evaluated; then assignTo attributes on those components execute; then page expressions, the action attribute on <apex:page>, and all other getter and setter calls are evaluated; then the view state is created if the page contains an <apex:form>; and finally the resulting HTML is sent to the browser.
So the constructors and expressions on custom components come after the controller constructor and before the page's own expressions and action attribute — not after them.
This item is defective as scraped: the step the question asks you to look past — 'after this step' — was carried by a diagram that did not survive, so the question cannot be answered from the printed text alone. Treat it as a prompt to know the sequence above.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_controller_get_request.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_controller_lifecycle.htm

corrected.note: Key A stands, but the explanation gave the order backwards — it said custom-component constructors are evaluated after the page's expressions, action attributes, and method calls, while the Visualforce guide places them before. Also flagged: the stem refers to 'this step' from a diagram lost in scraping, so the item is unanswerable as printed.

question: A developer needs to create a service that will process an email sent to it and create an account and contact using the contents of the email as data for the records.How might a developer accomplish this requirement?
optionA: Use the Apex Inbound Email Handler
optionB: Use the Fuel API with Email Data Extensions
optionC: Use Heroku Data Clips to Process Email
optionD: Use Auto-launched Flow and Process Builder
explanation:
An Apex class implementing the Messaging.InboundEmailHandler interface (an Apex email service) receives an inbound email, parses its contents, and can create records such as the Account and Contact from the email data. The Fuel API (B) is Marketing Cloud, Heroku Data Clips (C) run read-only SQL on Heroku Postgres, and Flow/Process Builder (D) can't directly receive inbound email.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_email_inbound.htm

question: How can Apex be used with Visual Workflow?
optionA: To set the version of a Flow being run
optionB: To start a Flow automatically
optionC: To add custom styling to a Flow
optionD: To control access to a Flow
explanation:
Apex can launch a flow programmatically using the Flow.Interview class (for example, starting a flow automatically from a trigger or controller). It can't set a flow's version (A), add styling (C), or control access to a flow (D) through Apex. Conversely, a flow can call Apex via an @InvocableMethod.

question: An integration user makes a successful login() call via the SOAP API.What can be used in the SOAP header to provide server authorization for subsequent API requests?
optionA: Named Credentials
optionB: Session ID
optionC: OAuth access token
optionD: Security token
explanation:
After a successful SOAP API login() call, Salesforce returns a session ID, and subsequent API requests authenticate by passing that session ID in the SOAP header (SessionHeader). Named Credentials (A) are for outbound Apex callouts, an OAuth access token (C) belongs to OAuth flows, and the security token (D) is appended to the password during login rather than used for per-request authorization.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api.meta/api/sforce_api_header_sessionheader.htm

question: A developer is creating unit tests for code that makes SOAP web service callouts. The developer needs to insert some test data as a part of the unit tests setup.What are three actions to enable this functionality? (Choose three.)
optionA: Surround the callout with Test.startTest(), Test.stopTest()
optionB: Surround the data insertion with Test.startTest(), Test.stopTest()
optionC: Implement the WebServiceMock interface
optionD: Update code to call Test.setMock()
explanation:
For a SOAP callout the mock is the WebServiceMock interface (C), registered with Test.setMock(WebServiceMock.class, new MyMock()) (D), and the callout itself goes inside Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest() (A). HttpCalloutMock is the equivalent for HTTP and REST callouts, not for a class generated from a WSDL, so E is the wrong interface here.
B is wrong because the data insertion belongs outside the start/stop block. A callout can't run while there is pending DML in the same transaction, and enclosing the callout — not the DML — is what allows both in one test method. Note that Test.startTest() does not commit anything: nothing in a test is ever committed. It opens a fresh context with its own set of governor limits, and that is the boundary the callout restriction is measured against.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_wsdl2apex_testing.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_interface_webservicemock.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_restful_http_testing_dml.htm

corrected.note: Answer A,C,D stands. The explanation asserted that wrapping the callout in Test.startTest()/Test.stopTest() means the data inserted beforehand 'is committed', which is false — a test never commits DML. Rewritten to say what the boundary actually does, and to state why HttpCalloutMock is the wrong interface for a WSDL-generated SOAP callout.

question: A developer has written an After Update trigger on Account. A workflow rule and field update cause the trigger to repeatedly update the Account records.How should the developer handle the recursive trigger?
optionA: Deactivate the trigger and move the logic into a Process or Flow
optionB: Deactivate the workflow rule to prevent the field update from executing
optionC: Use a static variable to prevent the trigger from executing more than once
optionD: Use a global variable to prevent the trigger from executing more than once
explanation:
A static variable in a helper class keeps its value for the whole transaction, so setting a boolean flag the first time the trigger runs and checking it afterward stops the workflow field update from re-firing the trigger endlessly. Deactivating the trigger or workflow (A/B) removes needed functionality, and a non-static ("global") variable (D) is reinstantiated and wouldn't persist across the recursive calls.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_static.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_bestpract.htm

question:
A developer has a page with two extensions overriding the Standard controller for Case.

```html
<apex:page standardController="Case" extension="CaseExtensionOne,CaseExtension Two" showHeader="false">
```

Each extension has a method called Save. The page has a command button as defined:

```html
<apex:commandButton value="Save" action="{!save}"/>
```
optionA: All of the three Save methods will be executed
optionB: Save from Case Standard Controller will be executed
optionC: Save from CaseExtensionTwo will be executed
optionD: Save from CaseExtensionOne will be executed
explanation:
With more than one extension on the same standard controller, a method defined in several places resolves to the leftmost extension — the one that appears first in the comma-separated extensions list. The Visualforce guide states this and gives the same shape of example: with extensions="ExtOne,ExtTwo" and getFoo() defined in both, the rendered value comes from ExtOne. So the Save in CaseExtensionOne is the one that runs, and only that one: the other extension's Save and the standard controller's Save are overridden rather than chained.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_controller_extension.htm

question: Choose the correct definition for <apex:actionSupport>.

optionB: Sends an AJAX request according to the time interval you specify. If this ever gets re-rendered, it resets

question: Choose the correct definition for <apex:messages>.
optionA: Standard Salesforce formatting, throws a specific message on a page
optionB: Standard Salesforce formatting, shows all errors that occur on page. Can add more messages through the "ApexPages.addMessage" function
optionC: single message, without formatting, that can be associated with a specific component on the page
optionD: No formatting; displays all errors on a page
explanation:
<apex:messages> displays all messages/errors generated for the page using standard Salesforce formatting, and you can add your own with ApexPages.addMessage(). It differs from <apex:message>, which shows a single, unformatted message tied to a specific component.

question: Which of the following standard fields are indexed? (Choose three.)
optionA: Name
optionB: CreatedBy
optionC: SystemModStamp
optionD: LastModifedDdate
explanation:
Salesforce maintains indexes on a documented set of standard fields: RecordTypeId, Division, CreatedDate, Systemmodstamp, Name, Email (on contacts and leads), lookup and master-detail foreign keys, and the record Id, which is the primary key for every object. Of the choices, Name, SystemModstamp, and RecordType appear on that list without qualification, so those are the three to pick.
CreatedBy is not on it. What carries the index is CreatedDate, the timestamp — not CreatedById.
One caveat about the remaining option. The Large Data Volumes guide writes that entry as "Systemmodstamp (LastModifiedDate)", treating the two as the same index rather than presenting LastModifiedDate as unindexed. So LastModifiedDate is not a clean distractor: this item works because the three fields named above are unambiguous, not because filtering on LastModifiedDate is documented to miss an index.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm
